title: Polity Lec 1
summary: The Constituent Assembly took 2 years, 11 months and 18 days to frame the Constitution; adopted on 26 November 1949, came into force on 26 January 1950; first meeting on 9 December 1946 (211 members).

From Canada: federation with a strong Centre, residuary powers with the Centre, appointment of Governors by the Centre (trick: C for Centre, C for Canada). From Britain: parliamentary system, single citizenship, FPTP, bicameralism. Amendment procedure from South Africa.

Article 368 (Part XX): only two types of amendment - by special majority, and by special majority plus ratification by at least half of the states (simple majority in state legislatures); citizenship, Legislative Councils etc. are changed by simple majority.

Federalism = division of powers between Centre and States; India is a 'federation with a strong Centre': K.C. Wheare (quasi-federal), Granville Austin (cooperative), Morris Jones (bargaining), Ivor Jennings (centralising tendency); Article 371A Nagaland = asymmetric federalism.

Unitary features: single citizenship, single Constitution, integrated judiciary, appointment of Governors, residuary powers, All India Services (Art. 312: IAS, IPS, IFoS). Federal features: Rajya Sabha, dual polity, division of powers.

Schedules: originally 8, now 12; 2nd - emoluments, 3rd - oaths (ministers here), 4th - Rajya Sabha seats, 5th - Scheduled Areas, 6th - Assam, Tripura, Meghalaya, Mizoram (ATM-M), 7th - three lists, 8th - 22 languages, 9th - 1951, 10th - 52nd Amendment (1985), 11th - 73rd (29 subjects), 12th - 74th (18 subjects).
Languages: 14 to 22 - Sindhi (21st Amendment), Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali (71st), Bodo, Dogri, Santhali, Maithili (92nd).

Seventh Schedule: Union 97→100, State 66→61, Concurrent 47→52 subjects; the 42nd Amendment moved 5 subjects (education, forests, weights and measures, protection of wild animals and birds, administration of justice) from State to Concurrent List; in case of conflict, the law of Parliament prevails (Art. 254).

Parts of the Constitution: 22 originally, now 25 (Part VII deleted); Part III Fundamental Rights, Part IV DPSP, Part V Union, Part VI States, Parts IX/IXA/IXB Panchayats/Municipalities/Co-operative Societies (97th, 2011), Part XI Centre-State relations, Part XII Finance and Property, Part XVI SC/ST, Part XVII Official Language, Part XX Amendment, Part XXI Special Provisions.

Preamble: borrowed from the USA; based on the Objectives Resolution (moved 13 December 1946, adopted 22 January 1947); Palkhivala - 'identity card', K.M. Munshi - 'political horoscope'; order - Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic; 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity' added by the 42nd Amendment (1976).

Preamble: Berubari (1960) - not a part of the Constitution; Kesavananda Bharati (1973) - a part, and amendable; Justice 3 types, Liberty 5, Equality 2, Fraternity 1; Justice from the Russian Revolution, Liberty-Equality-Fraternity from the French Revolution.

Fundamental Rights: Arts. 12-35, from 7 to 6 (Art. 31 deleted by the 44th Amendment, 1978); Equality 14-18, Freedom 19-22, against Exploitation 23-24, Religion 25-28, Cultural and Educational 29-30, Constitutional Remedies 32; Art. 12 defines 'State', Art. 13 makes inconsistent laws void; Equality includes Rule of Law (Dicey, Britain) and equal protection (USA).

Reservation: 15(4) by 1st Amendment 1951 (Champakam case), 15(6)/16(6) EWS by 103rd (2019), 16(4A) promotions by 77th, 16(4B) carry forward by 81st; Indra Sawhney 1992 - 50% ceiling, creamy layer; Kaka Kalelkar Commission 1953, Mandal Commission 1979 (implemented 1990).

Art. 19(1) has 6 freedoms; 19(2) restrictions (3 added by 1st Amendment - Romesh Thappar); Art. 20 - no ex post facto law, no double jeopardy, no self-incrimination; Art. 21 - procedure from Japan, Maneka Gandhi 1978 (due process), 21A (86th, 2002), privacy (Puttaswamy 2017); Arts. 20-21 cannot be suspended even in an emergency; Art. 22 - 24 hours, preventive detention 3 months.

Religious rights: 25 individuals, 26 religious denominations, 27 no tax for promotion of a religion, 28 no religious instruction in wholly state-funded institutions; 29-30 minorities ('minority' not defined); 31A/31B and Ninth Schedule (I.R. Coelho 2007: laws added after 24 April 1973 open to review); Art. 32 'heart and soul' (Ambedkar), five writs, Art. 226 (High Courts) wider; Arts. 33-35; property now under Art. 300A.

mcqs.q: Which example best shows the need for a constitution in daily life?
o: Setting rules for representation and sharing of resources
Buying groceries from a local shop
mcqs.e: A constitution lays down the basic rules, such as representation and sharing of resources.

mcqs.q: Creating a body of laws that limits and checks the powers of government is called:
mcqs.e: Constitutionalism means limits and checks on governmental power.

mcqs.q: How much time did the Constituent Assembly of India take to frame the Constitution?
mcqs.e: The Constitution took 2 years, 11 months and 18 days to frame.

mcqs.q: Which statement about an unwritten constitution, compared with a written one, is correct?
o: It is very difficult to amend
It is codified by a Constituent Assembly
It has no rules or conventions
It is relatively easy to amend
mcqs.e: An unwritten constitution rests on conventions and is easier to change; the UK is an example.

mcqs.q: Which country is the prime example of an unwritten constitution?
mcqs.e: The British constitution is regarded as unwritten, based largely on conventions.

mcqs.q: Which of the following features of the Indian Constitution was NOT borrowed from Britain?
o: Appointment of state Governors by the Centre
mcqs.e: Appointment of Governors by the Centre was borrowed from Canada.

mcqs.q: The provision for appointment of state Governors by the Centre is borrowed from the constitution of:
mcqs.e: From Canada: strong Centre, residuary powers with the Centre, appointment of Governors (C for Centre, C for Canada).

mcqs.q: The concept of a 'federation with a strong Centre' was borrowed from:
mcqs.e: Federation with a strong Centre was taken from the Canadian constitution.

mcqs.q: The provision vesting residuary powers in the Centre is borrowed from:
mcqs.e: Subjects not in any of the three lists are residuary; Parliament legislates on them.

mcqs.q: India adopted the First Past the Post (FPTP) electoral system from:
mcqs.e: FPTP, parliamentary system, single citizenship and bicameralism come from Britain.

mcqs.q: The largest part of the Indian Constitution is derived from:
mcqs.e: The bulk of the Constitution, including the administrative framework, came from the GoI Act 1935.

mcqs.q: India borrowed the procedure for amendment of the Constitution from:
mcqs.e: The amendment procedure (and election of Rajya Sabha members) was taken from South Africa.

mcqs.q: Amendment of the Constitution is dealt with under which Part and Article?
mcqs.e: Part XX (Article 368) lays down the amendment procedure.

mcqs.q: How many types of amendment are recognised under Article 368?
mcqs.e: Special majority, and special majority plus ratification by half the states; simple-majority changes are outside Art. 368.

mcqs.q: Which of the following can be changed by simple majority, outside the procedure of Article 368?
o: Manner of election of the President
mcqs.e: Citizenship (Art. 11), creation/abolition of Legislative Councils (Art. 169) and new states (Arts. 2-4) need a simple majority.

mcqs.q: What majority is required in Parliament for the creation or abolition of a state Legislative Council?
o: Special majority and ratification by half the states
Ratification by two-thirds of the states
mcqs.e: Under Article 169; it is not deemed an amendment under Article 368.

mcqs.q: Which amendment requires a special majority of Parliament along with ratification by at least half of the state legislatures (Art. 368(2))?
o: Manner of election of the President (Art. 55)
mcqs.e: Amendments affecting the federal structure need ratification by half the states; MLAs also vote in the presidential election.

mcqs.q: What majority is required in state legislatures to ratify a constitutional amendment?
mcqs.e: States ratify by simple majority; Parliament needs a special majority.

mcqs.q: Which north-eastern state has been given special status under Article 371A?
mcqs.e: Article 371A makes special provisions for Nagaland, an example of asymmetric federalism.

mcqs.q: What is the basic meaning of federalism?
o: Separation of powers among the three organs
Concentration of all powers in the Centre
Giving power only to the states
Division of powers between the Centre and the states
mcqs.e: Federalism is division of powers between Union and States; sharing among organs is separation of powers.

mcqs.q: Who described Indian federalism as 'quasi-federal'?
mcqs.e: K.C. Wheare called India quasi-federal.

mcqs.q: Who described Indian federalism as 'cooperative federalism'?
mcqs.e: Granville Austin: cooperative federalism.

mcqs.q: Who described Indian federalism as 'bargaining federalism'?
mcqs.e: Morris Jones: bargaining federalism.

mcqs.q: Who used the phrase 'a federation with a centralising tendency'?
mcqs.e: Ivor Jennings called the Indian union a federation with a centralising tendency.

mcqs.q: Granting some states more powers or special provisions than others reflects which form of Indian federalism?
mcqs.e: Article 371 (371A etc.) makes special provisions for various states.

mcqs.q: Why is the parliamentary system called the 'Westminster model'?
o: The British Parliament is located at Westminster
It was borrowed from the USA
It was created by the Treaty of Westminster
mcqs.e: India took the parliamentary system from Britain; it rests on accountability.

mcqs.q: What is the main basis of the parliamentary system?
o: Accountability of the executive to the legislature (Lok Sabha)
mcqs.e: The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha and falls if it loses majority.

mcqs.q: In which country does the presidential system of government operate?
mcqs.e: The USA has a presidential system with strict separation of powers; India does not.

mcqs.q: What are the three organs of government?
o: Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, Vidhan Sabha
mcqs.e: Legislature makes laws, executive implements them, judiciary interprets and reviews them.

mcqs.q: Why is there no strict separation of powers in India?
o: The executive is drawn from the legislature itself
mcqs.e: Ministers are members of Parliament, and the PM can advise dissolution of the Lok Sabha.

mcqs.q: Which is the correct difference between 'separation of powers' and 'division of powers'?
o: Separation is between Centre and states; division is among the three organs
Both are only between Centre and states
Separation is among the three organs; division is between Centre and states (and local government)
Both are only among the three organs
mcqs.e: Separation: three organs; division: Centre, states (and local bodies after the 73rd/74th Amendments).

mcqs.q: Which amendments gave constitutional status to local self-government (Panchayats, Municipalities)?
mcqs.e: Both were passed in 1992 and came into force in 1993.

mcqs.q: How long did Atal Bihari Vajpayee's government of 1996 last?
mcqs.e: It fell for lack of majority, an example of accountability in a parliamentary system.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a unitary feature of the Indian Constitution?
o: Representation of states in the Rajya Sabha
mcqs.e: Integrated judiciary, single citizenship, single constitution, Governors, residuary powers and AIS are unitary features.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a federal feature of the Indian system?
o: Division of powers between Centre and states
mcqs.e: Written constitution, supremacy of constitution, dual polity, bicameralism and division of powers are federal features.

mcqs.q: Which of the following reflects a unitary rather than a federal feature?
o: Division of powers between Union and states
Single citizenship for the whole country
mcqs.e: Single citizenship, borrowed from Britain, is unitary; the USA has dual citizenship.

mcqs.q: All India Services are provided for under which Article?
mcqs.e: IAS, IPS and IFoS are All India Services; recruited by the Centre but serve state cadres.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an All India Service?
mcqs.e: IAS, IPS and IFoS are the only three All India Services.

mcqs.q: In a statement like 'The basic rules of a constitution are based only on popular customs', what does the word 'only' indicate?
o: A hint of the correct answer
An extreme keyword that often makes a statement false
mcqs.e: Words like only, always, never make statements extreme; constitutional rules are legally enforceable.

mcqs.q: Exam trick: in an MCQ, where is the answer most often found?
mcqs.e: Teacher's tip: the answer is likely among two similar or opposite options.

mcqs.q: Which Schedule of the Constitution divides subjects between the Union and the states?
mcqs.e: The Seventh Schedule contains the Union, State and Concurrent Lists.

mcqs.q: How many Schedules did the original Constitution have, and how many are there now?
mcqs.e: The Ninth to Twelfth Schedules were added later.

mcqs.q: What does the First Schedule contain?
o: Names and territories of states and Union Territories
mcqs.e: First Schedule: names and territorial extent of states and UTs.

mcqs.q: The Second Schedule deals with the emoluments of:
o: President, Governors, judges, CAG, Speaker and Chairman
mcqs.e: Second Schedule = emoluments; ministers' salaries are not included.

mcqs.q: What does the Third Schedule contain?
mcqs.e: Third Schedule has oaths of ministers, judges etc.; the President's oath is in Article 60.

mcqs.q: The form of oath for Union ministers is given in which Schedule?
mcqs.e: Ministers' oaths are in the Third Schedule; their salaries are fixed by Parliament by law.

mcqs.q: Allocation of Rajya Sabha seats to the states is given in which Schedule?
mcqs.e: Fourth Schedule: allocation of seats in the Rajya Sabha.

mcqs.q: Administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes is described in which Schedule?
mcqs.e: Fifth Schedule: Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes.

mcqs.q: The Sixth Schedule provides for administration of tribal areas in which states?
mcqs.e: Trick ATM-M: Assam, Tripura, Meghalaya, Mizoram; Manipur is not included.

mcqs.q: In Sixth Schedule areas, which councils enjoy legislative, judicial and financial powers?
mcqs.e: ADCs can make laws, run local courts and levy taxes; Ladakh has been demanding Sixth Schedule status.

mcqs.q: Which council formed in Fifth Schedule areas is only advisory?
mcqs.e: The TAC is advisory; Fifth Schedule areas currently exist in 10 states.

mcqs.q: Who has the power to declare Scheduled Areas under the Fifth Schedule?
mcqs.e: The President declares Fifth Schedule areas; state names are not listed in the Schedule.

mcqs.q: The list of languages is given in which Schedule of the Constitution?
mcqs.e: The Eighth Schedule had 14 languages originally; now 22.

mcqs.q: How many languages did the Eighth Schedule originally contain, and how many now?
mcqs.e: Eight languages were added later.

mcqs.q: Sindhi was added to the Eighth Schedule by which amendment?
mcqs.e: Sindhi was added by the 21st Amendment.

mcqs.q: Konkani, Nepali and Manipuri were added to the Eighth Schedule by which amendment?
mcqs.e: The 71st Amendment added Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali.

mcqs.q: Bodo, Dogri, Santhali and Maithili were added to the Eighth Schedule by which amendment?
mcqs.e: The 92nd Amendment added Bodo, Dogri, Santhali and Maithili.

mcqs.q: The Ninth Schedule was added by which amendment?
mcqs.e: It was added mainly to shield land reform laws from judicial review.

mcqs.q: The anti-defection law is in which Schedule and was added by which amendment?
mcqs.e: The Tenth Schedule was added by the 52nd Amendment, 1985.

mcqs.q: How many functional subjects for Panchayats are listed in the Eleventh Schedule?
mcqs.e: Eleventh Schedule: Panchayats, 29 subjects; added by the 73rd Amendment (1992), in force 1993.

mcqs.q: How many functional subjects for Municipalities are listed in the Twelfth Schedule?
mcqs.e: Twelfth Schedule: Municipalities, 18 subjects; added by the 74th Amendment (1992).

mcqs.q: The Twelfth Schedule was added by which amendment?
mcqs.e: The 74th Amendment was passed in 1992 and came into force in 1993.

mcqs.q: Which subjects fall in the Union List?
mcqs.e: Subjects of national importance needing uniformity are in the Union List; only Parliament legislates on them.

mcqs.q: Which of the following subjects is in the State List?
mcqs.e: State List: police/public order, land, agriculture etc.; state legislatures make laws on them.

mcqs.q: Which of the following subjects is in the Concurrent List?
mcqs.e: Concurrent List: education, marriage and divorce etc.; both Parliament and states can legislate.

mcqs.q: How many subjects did the Union List originally have, and how many now?
mcqs.e: Union List: 97 → 100 entries (as commonly cited).

mcqs.q: What is the present number of subjects in the State List?
mcqs.e: The State List originally had 66 subjects; 61 after the 42nd Amendment (as commonly cited).

mcqs.q: What is the present number of subjects in the Concurrent List?
mcqs.e: Concurrent List: originally 47, now 52.

mcqs.q: If both Parliament and a state legislature make a law on a Concurrent List subject, whose law prevails?
mcqs.e: Under Article 254 (doctrine of repugnancy), the law of Parliament prevails.

mcqs.q: When can a state law on a Concurrent List subject prevail in the state?
o: If it receives the President's assent
mcqs.e: If reserved for and assented to by the President, it prevails in that state, though Parliament can later override it.

mcqs.q: The 'doctrine of repugnancy' is contained in which Article?
mcqs.e: Art. 254: conflict between Central and state laws on the Concurrent List; Art. 248: residuary powers.

mcqs.q: How many subjects were transferred from the State List to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment?
mcqs.e: Education, forests, weights and measures, protection of wild animals and birds, administration of justice.

mcqs.q: Which of the following was NOT transferred from the State List to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment?
o: Protection of wild animals and birds
mcqs.e: Transferred: education, forests, weights and measures, wildlife protection, administration of justice.

mcqs.q: Who has the power to make laws on a subject not mentioned in any of the three lists?
mcqs.e: Residuary powers lie with the Centre (borrowed from Canada).

mcqs.q: Fundamental Rights are contained in which Part of the Constitution?
mcqs.e: Part III: Fundamental Rights; Part IV: DPSP; Part IVA: Fundamental Duties.

mcqs.q: What is described in Part IV of the Constitution?
mcqs.e: Part IV = DPSP; Part III = Fundamental Rights.

mcqs.q: Which Part of the Constitution deals with the Union executive?
mcqs.e: Part V deals with the Union, Part VI with the states.

mcqs.q: Special provisions for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and backward classes are in which Part?
mcqs.e: Part XVI (Arts. 330-342A): special provisions relating to certain classes.

mcqs.q: Provisions relating to the official language are in which Part of the Constitution?
mcqs.e: Part XVII: language of the Union, regional languages, language of courts, special directives.

mcqs.q: Articles 350 and 351 deal with:
mcqs.e: Chapter IV of Part XVII: special directives (mother-tongue instruction, development of Hindi).

mcqs.q: Provisions relating to Panchayats are in which Part of the Constitution?
mcqs.e: Part IX Panchayats, IXA Municipalities, IXB Co-operative Societies.

mcqs.q: Part IXB on co-operative societies was added by which amendment?
mcqs.e: Any question on co-operative societies: the answer is the 97th Amendment.

mcqs.q: Relations between the Union and the states (Arts. 245-263) are in which Part?
mcqs.e: Part XI = Centre-State relations.

mcqs.q: Finance, property, contracts and suits are the subject of which Part?
mcqs.e: Part XII covers finance, property, contracts and suits, including Art. 300A (right to property).

mcqs.q: Special provisions for certain states (such as Article 371) fall under which Part?
mcqs.e: Part XXI: temporary, transitional and special provisions; Part XX = amendment, Part XIX = miscellaneous.

mcqs.q: How many Parts did the Constitution originally have, and how many now?
mcqs.e: Four Parts were added (IVA, IXA, IXB, XIVA) and one (Part VII) was deleted.

mcqs.q: Which Part of the Constitution was deleted by the 7th Amendment?
mcqs.e: Part VII (Part B states) was deleted by the 7th Amendment, 1956.

mcqs.q: When was the Indian Constitution adopted and when did it come into force?
mcqs.e: 26 November is celebrated as Constitution Day.

mcqs.q: In what capacity does the Preamble function?
o: As a guiding principle for interpretation (essence of the Constitution)
As a law enforceable in courts
mcqs.e: The Preamble is the essence of the Constitution but is not enforceable in court.

mcqs.q: India borrowed the idea of the Preamble from the constitution of:
mcqs.e: The Preamble is from the USA; justice from the Russian Revolution, liberty-equality-fraternity from the French Revolution.

mcqs.q: Who called the Preamble the 'identity card of the Constitution'?
mcqs.e: N.A. Palkhivala: identity card of the Constitution.

mcqs.q: Who called the Preamble the 'political horoscope' of the Constitution?
mcqs.e: K.M. Munshi: political horoscope.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the Preamble is correct?
o: It cannot be enforced in a court of law
It is above the Fundamental Rights
It is part of the Fundamental Rights
mcqs.e: The Preamble is non-justiciable, but it can be amended (Kesavananda Bharati).

mcqs.q: The Preamble tells us about which four things?
o: Source of authority, nature of the state, objectives and date of adoption
mcqs.e: Source: We the people; nature: sovereign socialist secular democratic republic; objectives: justice etc.; date: 26 Nov 1949.

mcqs.q: According to the Preamble, what is the source of authority of the Constitution?
mcqs.e: 'We, the people of India' are the source of authority.

mcqs.q: What is the correct order of the words describing India in the Preamble?
mcqs.e: Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic - questions test this order.

mcqs.q: What does the word 'sovereign' in the Preamble mean?
mcqs.e: Sovereign: independent in decision-making, not subject to any external power.

mcqs.q: The word 'Socialist' was added to the Preamble by which amendment?
mcqs.e: The 42nd Amendment added Socialist, Secular and Integrity; it is called the 'mini-Constitution'.

mcqs.q: Which three words were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment?
mcqs.e: Trick SSI: Socialist, Secular, Integrity; 'Sovereign' was original.

mcqs.q: How many times has the Preamble been amended so far?
mcqs.e: Only once, by the 42nd Amendment (1976).

mcqs.q: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment is popularly known as:
mcqs.e: It made so many changes that it was called the 'mini-Constitution'.

mcqs.q: What does declaring India 'secular' in the Preamble mean?
o: The State protects all religions equally
The State has an official religion
Only the majority religion is protected
mcqs.e: India has no state religion (unlike, e.g., Pakistan, an Islamic state).

mcqs.q: Which word in the Preamble indicates that India's head of state is elected, not hereditary?
mcqs.e: Republic: elected head of state (indirectly in India); Britain has a hereditary monarchy.

mcqs.q: What is the main meaning of socialism?
o: Means of production in the hands of capitalists
Government control over the means of production
mcqs.e: Its opposite is capitalism.

mcqs.q: How many types of justice are mentioned in the Preamble?
mcqs.e: Social, economic and political justice, taken from the Russian Revolution.

mcqs.q: How many types of liberty are mentioned in the Preamble?
mcqs.e: Liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship.

mcqs.q: How many types of equality are mentioned in the Preamble?
mcqs.e: Equality of status and of opportunity.

mcqs.q: According to the Preamble, fraternity assures:
o: Dignity of the individual and unity and integrity of the Nation
mcqs.e: Fraternity has one type; 'integrity' was added by the 42nd Amendment.

mcqs.q: India took the ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity from which revolution?
mcqs.e: Social, economic and political justice was taken from the Russian Revolution.

mcqs.q: When is Constitution Day celebrated?
mcqs.e: The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949.

mcqs.q: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution?
mcqs.e: Berubari (1960): the Preamble is not part of the Constitution.

mcqs.q: In which case was the Preamble first held to be a part of the Constitution?
mcqs.e: This made amendment of the Preamble possible (42nd Amendment, 1976).

mcqs.q: The S.R. Bommai case is related to:
o: Whether the Preamble is part of the Constitution
mcqs.e: President's Rule must be a last resort and cannot be imposed arbitrarily.

mcqs.q: The Preamble is based on which resolution moved by Pandit Nehru?
mcqs.e: The Objectives Resolution is the basis of the Preamble, not the Preamble itself.

mcqs.q: When did Nehru move the Objectives Resolution in the Constituent Assembly, and when was it adopted?
mcqs.e: Moved on 13 December 1946 and adopted on 22 January 1947.

mcqs.q: When was the first meeting of the Constituent Assembly held, and how many members attended?
mcqs.e: The first meeting was held on 9 December 1946 with 211 members present.

mcqs.q: The 61st Constitutional Amendment is related to:
o: Lowering the voting age from 21 to 18 years
Lowering the voting age from 25 to 21
mcqs.e: The 61st Amendment (1988) lowered the voting age to 18.

mcqs.q: In which Part and Articles are Fundamental Rights placed, and from where were they borrowed?
o: Part III, Arts. 12-35; inspired by the US Bill of Rights
mcqs.e: Fundamental Rights are inspired by the American Bill of Rights.

mcqs.q: How many Fundamental Rights were there in the original Constitution, and how many now?
mcqs.e: The right to property (Art. 31) was removed by the 44th Amendment, 1978.

mcqs.q: The Right to Equality is contained in which Articles?
mcqs.e: Equality 14-18; Freedom 19-22; against Exploitation 23-24; Religion 25-28; Cultural-Educational 29-30; Remedies 32.

mcqs.q: The Right to Freedom is contained in which Articles?
mcqs.e: Articles 19 to 22 cover the Right to Freedom.

mcqs.q: The Right against Exploitation is described in which Articles?
mcqs.e: Art. 23 bans human trafficking and forced labour; Art. 24 bans employing children below 14 in hazardous work.

mcqs.q: The Right to Freedom of Religion is contained in which Articles?
mcqs.e: Articles 25 to 28 cover freedom of religion.

mcqs.q: Cultural and Educational Rights are contained in which Articles?
mcqs.e: Art. 29: protection of language, script and culture; Art. 30: educational institutions of minorities.

mcqs.q: The Right to Constitutional Remedies is contained in which Article?
mcqs.e: Art. 31 (property) has been deleted; Art. 226 is not a Fundamental Right.

mcqs.q: Which statement about Fundamental Rights is incorrect?
o: Reasonable restrictions can be imposed on them
They are absolute and cannot be restricted
Cultural and educational rights of Arts. 29-30 are also Fundamental Rights
mcqs.e: Fundamental Rights are not absolute; they are subject to reasonable restrictions.

mcqs.q: Article 12 defines which term?
mcqs.e: Parliament, state legislatures, Union/state governments, local bodies and other authorities are 'State'.

mcqs.q: Under Article 13, what happens to laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights?
o: Only the Governor can annul them
mcqs.e: Art. 13 is the basis of judicial review of both pre- and post-constitutional laws.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT included in the definition of 'State' under Article 12?
mcqs.e: Parliament, legislatures, Union and state governments and local authorities are included.

mcqs.q: 'Equality before law' and 'equal protection of laws' are contained in which Article?
mcqs.e: Article 14 contains both concepts.

mcqs.q: The concept of 'equality before law' was borrowed from which country, and what kind of concept is it?
mcqs.e: It is linked to the Rule of Law: no one is above the law.

mcqs.q: Who propounded the concept of 'Rule of Law'?
mcqs.e: A.V. Dicey gave the concept of Rule of Law.

mcqs.q: 'Equal protection of laws' is what kind of concept, and from where was it borrowed?
mcqs.e: It means like should be treated alike in similar circumstances.

mcqs.q: Article 15 prohibits the State from discriminating on which grounds?
o: Religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth
mcqs.e: Discrimination is barred only on these grounds.

mcqs.q: Under Article 15(2), access to which places cannot be denied?
o: Shops, public restaurants, hotels, wells, bathing ghats
mcqs.e: It guarantees access to public places.

mcqs.q: Article 15(3) allows the State to make special provisions for:
mcqs.e: Such provisions do not violate Article 15.

mcqs.q: Article 15(4) was added by which amendment?
mcqs.e: It enables special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes after Champakam Dorairajan (1951).

mcqs.q: Article 15(5) provides for:
o: Reservation for backward classes in educational institutions, including private ones
mcqs.e: Added by the 93rd Amendment, 2005; covers admissions in aided/unaided institutions except minority ones.

mcqs.q: Which amendment added Articles 15(6) and 16(6) to provide reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS)?
mcqs.e: EWS reservation: 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019.

mcqs.q: Article 16 is related to:
o: Equality of opportunity in public employment
mcqs.e: Equality of opportunity in public employment.

mcqs.q: Who can prescribe a residence requirement for certain posts in public employment (Art. 16(3))?
mcqs.e: Parliament may by law prescribe residence for posts in a state/UT.

mcqs.q: Article 16(4A), providing reservation in promotions, was added by which amendment?
mcqs.e: Indra Sawhney barred reservation in promotions; the 77th Amendment added 16(4A).

mcqs.q: The 'carry forward' rule in Article 16(4B) was added by which amendment?
mcqs.e: Allows unfilled reserved vacancies to be carried forward to later years.

mcqs.q: Under Article 16(5), what may be done for an office in a religious institution?
o: It applies only to government institutions
Belonging to that religion can be made a qualification
mcqs.e: Membership of the particular religion may be required for posts in religious/denominational bodies.

mcqs.q: Abolition of untouchability is provided in which Article?
mcqs.e: Art. 17: abolition of untouchability.

mcqs.q: In 1976, the Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955 was renamed as:
mcqs.e: Renamed the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 in 1976.

mcqs.q: Which Article prevents Indian citizens from accepting titles from a foreign state?
mcqs.e: Art. 18 abolishes titles; military and academic distinctions are exempt; Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are not titles.

mcqs.q: Which of the following does NOT count as a 'title' under Article 18?
o: Any title from a foreign state
mcqs.e: Bharat Ratna, Padma awards etc. are decorations; academic distinctions are also outside Art. 18.

mcqs.q: The right to reside and settle in any part of India is in which Article?
mcqs.e: Art. 19(1) has six freedoms: speech (a), assembly (b), association (c), movement (d), residence (e), profession (g).

mcqs.q: Article 19(1)(a) describes which right?
mcqs.e: Expression through any medium: newspapers, songs, pictures, etc.

mcqs.q: What condition applies to the freedom of assembly under Article 19(1)(b)?
mcqs.e: Citizens may assemble peaceably and without arms.

mcqs.q: Which sub-clause of Article 19(1) was deleted, and by which amendment?
mcqs.e: The 44th Amendment removed 19(1)(f) and Art. 31, making property a legal right under Art. 300A.

mcqs.q: What is the present status of the right to property?
mcqs.e: It is now a constitutional/legal right, not a Fundamental Right.

mcqs.q: Article 19(2) is related to:
mcqs.e: Grounds include public order, incitement, contempt, defamation, decency, sovereignty, security, friendly relations.

mcqs.q: Which three restrictions were added to Article 19(2) by the 1st Amendment (1951)?
o: Public order, friendly relations with foreign states, incitement to an offence
mcqs.e: Three grounds were added by the 1st Amendment; there are now eight grounds in all.

mcqs.q: Which case, in which a ban on a journal was lifted, prompted the 1st Constitutional Amendment of 1951?
o: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras
mcqs.e: Romesh Thappar (1950): the court lifted Madras's ban on the journal 'Cross Roads'.

mcqs.q: Which rights are suspended automatically only in an emergency on grounds of war/external aggression, not armed rebellion?
mcqs.e: Art. 358: Art. 19 is suspended in a war/external aggression emergency, not in armed rebellion.

mcqs.q: How many clauses does Article 20 have and what do they deal with?
o: Three: no ex post facto law, no double jeopardy, no self-incrimination
mcqs.e: Art. 20: protection in respect of conviction for offences.

mcqs.q: What does 'no ex post facto law' mean?
o: No double punishment for one offence
The accused cannot be made a witness against himself
Only the penalty in force at the time of the offence applies, not one enhanced later
mcqs.e: Article 20(1).

mcqs.q: What does 'no double jeopardy' mean?
o: No law will be made after the offence
No punishment twice for the same offence
mcqs.e: Article 20(2).

mcqs.q: What is the exception to the protection against self-incrimination?
o: One may have to give blood samples, handwriting and thumb impressions
mcqs.e: Art. 20(3) bars compelled testimony, but not blood samples, thumb impressions or handwriting.

mcqs.q: Under Article 21, a person can be deprived of life and personal liberty only:
o: According to procedure established by law
mcqs.e: 'Procedure established by law' was borrowed from the Japanese constitution.

mcqs.q: The concept of 'procedure established by law' was borrowed from:
mcqs.e: Art. 21 takes it from Japan; the USA has 'due process of law'.

mcqs.q: In which case did the Supreme Court give a narrow interpretation of Article 21?
mcqs.e: Gopalan looked only at the validity of procedure; Maneka Gandhi adopted a wider due-process approach.

mcqs.q: Which case, decided during the Emergency, is known as the Habeas Corpus case?
mcqs.e: The court held habeas corpus unavailable while Art. 21 was suspended; the 44th Amendment later protected Arts. 20-21.

mcqs.q: In which case did the Supreme Court adopt the idea of 'due process of law', requiring laws to be just, fair and reasonable?
o: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
mcqs.e: Maneka Gandhi's passport was impounded; the right to go abroad was read into Art. 21.

mcqs.q: The right to go abroad has been held to be a part of which Article?
mcqs.e: Held under Art. 21 in the Maneka Gandhi case.

mcqs.q: Rights under which Articles cannot be suspended even during a National Emergency?
mcqs.e: Since the 44th Amendment (1978), Arts. 20 and 21 cannot be suspended in an emergency.

mcqs.q: The right to free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14 was provided by which Article and amendment?
mcqs.e: Article 21A was inserted by the 86th Amendment, 2002.

mcqs.q: In which case was the right to privacy declared a Fundamental Right in 2017?
o: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (Aadhaar case)
mcqs.e: The right to privacy is part of Article 21.

mcqs.q: What was struck down in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India?
mcqs.e: A 2015 free-speech (Art. 19) case.

mcqs.q: What happened in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018)?
o: Section 377 IPC struck down to the extent it criminalised homosexuality
mcqs.e: Consensual same-sex relations were decriminalised.

mcqs.q: Under Article 22, within how much time must an arrested person (ordinary arrest) be produced before a magistrate?
mcqs.e: Within 24 hours, excluding travel time.

mcqs.q: For how long at most can a person be held in preventive detention without the opinion of an Advisory Board?
mcqs.e: Beyond that, an Advisory Board of High Court judges must approve; the 44th Amendment's change was never notified.

mcqs.q: Which clauses of Article 22 deal with punitive (ordinary) arrest and which with preventive detention?
o: All clauses deal only with preventive detention
All clauses deal only with punitive arrest
mcqs.e: Clauses 1-2 cover ordinary arrest, clause 3 sets exceptions, clauses 4-7 cover preventive detention.

mcqs.q: In Vihaan Kumar v. State of Haryana (2025), why did the Supreme Court declare the arrest illegal?
o: He was not produced within 24 hours
Grounds of arrest were not communicated (Art. 22)
mcqs.e: Art. 22(1) mandates informing the grounds of arrest and the right to consult a lawyer.

mcqs.q: Article 25 describes which right?
o: Freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion
Right of denominations to establish institutions
mcqs.e: Art. 25 is an individual right, subject to public order, health and morality.

mcqs.q: Article 26 confers rights on:
mcqs.e: Art. 26: establish/maintain institutions, manage religious affairs, own and administer property.

mcqs.q: Which right is NOT available to religious denominations under Article 26?
o: Compelling people to pay taxes for promotion of their religion
mcqs.e: Art. 27: no one can be compelled to pay taxes for promoting any religion.

mcqs.q: Under Article 28, religious instruction cannot be given in:
o: Educational institutions wholly maintained out of State funds
mcqs.e: Art. 28 bars religious instruction in wholly state-funded institutions.

mcqs.q: What right does Article 29 provide?
o: Right of any section of citizens to conserve its language, script and culture
Right of minorities to establish educational institutions
mcqs.e: Art. 29(2): no denial of admission to state-aided institutions on grounds of religion, race, caste or language.

mcqs.q: Which Article gives minorities (religious and linguistic) the right to establish and administer educational institutions?
mcqs.e: The term 'minority' is not defined anywhere in the Constitution.

mcqs.q: Article 31B was introduced to protect which kind of laws from judicial challenge?
mcqs.e: Arts. 31A and 31B were added by the 1st Amendment; Ninth Schedule laws were shielded from review.

mcqs.q: What did the Supreme Court hold in the I.R. Coelho case (2007)?
o: Review of all laws is barred
Laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 are open to judicial review
mcqs.e: The Ninth Schedule case, based on Kesavananda Bharati (1973): judicial review is part of the basic structure.

mcqs.q: What doctrine did the Supreme Court lay down in the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973)?
o: Preamble is not part of the Constitution
Parliament can take away Fundamental Rights
mcqs.e: Parliament cannot alter the basic structure; judicial review is part of it.

mcqs.q: Who called Article 32 the 'heart and soul of the Constitution'?
mcqs.e: It is the means of protecting Fundamental Rights.

mcqs.q: How many types of writs can the Supreme Court issue under Article 32?
mcqs.e: Habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto.

mcqs.q: High Courts derive their power to issue writs from which Article?
mcqs.e: Art. 226 is not a Fundamental Right; a High Court may decline a writ, while Art. 32 itself is a Fundamental Right.

mcqs.q: Why is the writ jurisdiction of High Courts wider than that of the Supreme Court?
o: They can issue writs for both Fundamental Rights and other legal rights
Because they are under the President
Because they issue writs only in state matters
Because they deal only with legal rights
mcqs.e: The Supreme Court issues writs under Art. 32 only for violation of Fundamental Rights.

mcqs.q: What is meant by the writ of 'mandamus'?
o: 'We command' - an order to a public official to perform a duty
Quash an order of a subordinate court
mcqs.e: Mandamus orders a public official or body to perform a mandatory duty.

mcqs.q: The writ of 'prohibition' is issued by whom and against whom?
o: By a lower court against a higher court
By the President against a court
By a higher court against a subordinate court, to stop it exceeding jurisdiction
mcqs.e: It stops the proceedings while they are still pending.

mcqs.q: What does the writ of 'certiorari' do?
o: Releases a person from illegal detention
Questions the authority of an office holder
Compels an official to perform a duty
Quashes an order passed by a subordinate court beyond its jurisdiction, transferring the case to itself
mcqs.e: Prohibition prevents excess of jurisdiction; certiorari cures it after the order is passed.

mcqs.q: Which writ protects life and personal liberty against illegal arrest or detention?
mcqs.e: Habeas corpus means 'to have the body'.

mcqs.q: Does the principle of 'locus standi' apply to habeas corpus?
o: Yes, only the aggrieved person can file
No, any other person can also file the petition
Yes, only a lawyer can file
mcqs.e: Locus standi means only the aggrieved may approach the court; it is relaxed for habeas corpus.

mcqs.q: Parliament's power to restrict or modify the application of Fundamental Rights to the armed forces comes from which Article?
mcqs.e: Art. 33: armed forces, police forces etc.

mcqs.q: What does Article 34 provide?
o: Restriction of Fundamental Rights for armed forces
Only Parliament legislates on Fundamental Rights
Restriction of Fundamental Rights while martial law is in force
mcqs.e: Art. 34: restrictions on rights in areas under martial law.

mcqs.q: Under Article 35, the power to make laws to give effect to certain Fundamental Rights lies only with:
mcqs.e: Art. 35: only Parliament.

mcqs.q: In what context did the Supreme Court call itself the 'sentinel on the qui vive'?
mcqs.e: State of Madras v. V.G. Row (1952).

mcqs.q: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights?
mcqs.e: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) later allowed amendment, but not of the basic structure.

mcqs.q: What did the court decide in the Indra Sawhney case (Mandal case, 1992)?
o: OBC reservation valid, creamy layer excluded, total reservation not to exceed 50%
mcqs.e: It also barred reservation in promotions (reversed by the 77th Amendment) and struck down the 10% economic quota.

mcqs.q: Under whose chairmanship was the first Backward Classes Commission (1953) set up, whose recommendations were not implemented?
mcqs.e: The second was the Mandal Commission (1979); V.P. Singh's government implemented it in 1990.

mcqs.q: Under which Prime Minister were the Mandal Commission recommendations implemented?
mcqs.e: The Mandal Commission was set up in 1979; the Indra Sawhney case challenged its implementation.

mcqs.q: The Anuradha Bhasin case is related to:
mcqs.e: Freedom of speech and trade via the internet is protected under Art. 19; decided in 2020.

mcqs.q: The Raj Narain v. Indira Gandhi (1975) case was related to:
mcqs.e: The Allahabad High Court set aside her election from Rae Bareli; the Emergency followed.
